question:
Patient note:
A 57-year-old woman is interviewed in the orthopedic holding bay this morning just before transport to the laminar-flow suite for a planned left total hip replacement that the attending surgeon anticipates will last about two and a half hours under general anesthesia with cemented fixation and postoperative weight-bearing as tolerated. Three weeks ago she was in a different operating room for an open abdominal myomectomy that required a midline infra-umbilical incision and an overnight stay; convalescence from that procedure went smoothly, and she resumed her usual eight-block dog-walks within ten days, climbing the two flights to her apartment without pauses, so baseline ambulation has returned to normal and she arrives today on her own two feet carrying a small canvas tote. Her medical history is notable for a nonischemic dilated cardiomyopathy diagnosed five years ago after a viral syndrome; resting echocardiography last month showed an ejection fraction of 38 %, and nine days ago dietary indiscretion led to five pounds of fluid weight with nocturnal orthopnea that prompted an emergency-department visit where intravenous furosemide and a single dose of intravenous nitroglycerin were administered with rapid symptom relief; she has had no breathlessness or lower-extremity edema since and takes carvedilol 25 mg twice daily, lisinopril 20 mg, and a morning dose of torsemide 20 mg. Ten years earlier, following a transatlantic flight, she developed aching behind the right knee and duplex ultrasonography revealed an occlusive thrombus in the popliteal vein; she completed six months of warfarin and has remained clot-free since, although chronic serpiginous superficial veins are visible along both medial calves, more pronounced after prolonged standing but never treated with ablation or stockings. She denies prior pulmonary embolism, stroke-like episodes, spinal cord injury, recent fractures, casts, splints, or high-energy trauma. No relative has been told of an inherited clotting disorder, and she herself has never tested positive for lupus anticoagulant, prothrombin mutation, or similar. She has never carried diagnoses of chronic lung disease, inflammatory bowel pathology, active or historical cancer, or systemic infection requiring intensive care; her last chest radiograph six months ago for routine surveillance was clear. She has not had any respiratory infections—including pneumonia—nor any systemic infectious episodes suggestive of sepsis within the past month. Medications stopped five days ago per protocol include her daily 81 mg aspirin; she has never taken hormone replacement therapy, erythropoiesis-stimulating agents, glucocorticoids, or selective estrogen-receptor modulators. She quit smoking two decades ago after a 15-pack-year history, drinks a glass of wine on holidays, and her body mass index this morning is 26 kg m⁻². On inspection she appears comfortable, answers questions in full sentences, and is oriented; Mallampati class II airway with intact dentition and full cervical extension is noted. Vital signs recorded ten minutes ago show temperature 36.6 °C, blood pressure 128/74 mm Hg, pulse 78 beats min⁻¹ in regular rhythm, respirations 14 min⁻¹, and oxygen saturation 98 % on ambient air. Jugular venous pressure is not elevated, carotid pulses are brisk, S₁ and S₂ are crisp without murmurs, gallops, or rubs, and lungs are clear to auscultation bilaterally. The abdomen bears a well-healing 12-cm midline scar with intact staples and no tenderness. Examination of the lower limbs reveals warm skin, palpable dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses 2+, thin-walled tortuous veins coursing over both calves, calf circumferences symmetric at 34 cm, and no pitting or brawny edema; the left hip demonstrates painful restriction of internal rotation consistent with end-stage osteoarthritis, while motor strength in all other muscle groups is 5/5. Neurologic screen shows intact sensation and reflexes. Only a single 18-gauge peripheral IV in the right forearm is running lactated Ringer’s at keep-open rate; there are no ports, tunneled catheters, or peripherally inserted central lines. Morning laboratory studies reveal hemoglobin 12.8 g dL⁻¹, hematocrit 38 %, platelet count 236 × 10⁹ L⁻¹, leukocytes 6.4 × 10⁹ L⁻¹, sodium 137 mmol L⁻¹, potassium 4.1 mmol L⁻¹, bicarbonate 24 mmol L⁻¹, creatinine 0.88 mg dL⁻¹, AST 20 U L⁻¹, ALT 18 U L⁻¹, total bilirubin 0.7 mg dL⁻¹, prothrombin time 12.2 s with international normalized ratio 1.0, and activated partial thromboplastin time 30 s. A baseline 12-lead electrocardiogram shows normal sinus rhythm at 76 beats min⁻¹, QRS duration 92 ms, and no acute ST-T changes compared with the tracing from her heart-failure follow-up. Posterior–anterior chest radiography obtained on arrival depicts clear lung fields and a stable cardiomediastinal silhouette without vascular congestion. Sequential calf compression sleeves are already wrapped but remain uninflated pending induction, and no pharmacologic antithrombotic has yet been given while the anesthesia team completes sign-in and formulates an intra-operative hemodynamic plan. She has been nil per os since midnight, removed jewelry and contact lenses, last voided an hour ago, and articulates understanding of the operative steps, potential need for transfusion, and the importance of early postoperative mobilization.

Question: What is the patient's Caprini Score for Venous Thromboembolism?
solution:
The Caprini VTE score adds weighted perioperative risk factors. The qualifying factors are:
- Age 41–60 years: age 57, 1 point.
- BMI >25 kg/m²: BMI 26, 1 point.
- Visible varicose veins: tortuous superficial calf veins, 1 point.
- Heart failure within the past month: symptomatic exacerbation nine days ago, 1 point.
- Major surgery within the past month: open abdominal myomectomy three weeks ago, 1 point.
- Personal history of VTE: prior popliteal DVT, 3 points, even though it was provoked and remote.
- Planned elective hip arthroplasty: 5 points. Do not also count the same operation as generic major surgery.
She is ambulatory without current leg swelling. Total = 1 + 1 + 1 + 1 + 1 + 3 + 5 = 13.
Final answer: 13
